#128195. SEO For AI Crawlers: How to serve AI Agent friendly pages?

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (928 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

SEO For AI Crawlers: How to serve AI Agent friendly pages?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that AI-friendly pages are plain-text (usually markdown) versions of webpages that are meant for AI, rather than people.
  • Industry observers note that we ran this test at acme.bot on November 4, 2026, across 53 live pages on 43 host names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that AI-friendly pages are plain-text (usually markdown) versions of webpages that are meant for AI, rather than people. Websites typically determine that AI is requesting a page via the user agent, Accept header, or a specific .md URL.

Industry observers note that we ran this test at acme.bot on November 4, 2026, across 53 live pages on 43 host names. Because we targeted sites likely to do this, the sample leans towards developer tools.

While testing the HubSpot, Gymshark, Semrush and Profound web pages, we didn't find any markdown on the pages.

While it's a common practice in developer documentation, there's not much research or evidence that it helps AI visibility.

Dries Buytaert checked a month of Cloudflare logs and found no AI crawler using content negotiation. The crawlers reached his markdown only through dedicated URLs, by following an auto-discovery link. So a site that relies on Accept alone is serving coding agents - and, possibly, no crawlers at all.

It has been revealed that even when the request asks for HTML, Stripe's docs still send markdown to all six AI user agents we tested. They send HTML to Bingbot, Googlebot, and browsers. The Checkout page drops from 846 KB to 5.5 KB. Its markdown has links to other .md pages, keeping an agent in the text pages. The response to markdown comes with the header X-Robots-Tag: none to ensure it is kept out of search indexes. Sentry's docs route the same way.

Vercel pages (including the blog and pricing page) that we tried all returned markdown on request. Docs pages also go to AI user agents, unless the request prefers HTML. Pricing and blog pages do not. The Next.js docs exhibit a similar behavior.

Neon delivers markdown on docs and pricing to non-browser clients that do not prefer HTML, including plain curl.

Neon's page isn't just a conversion. The markdown copy of its introduction is about 3,070 words, against roughly 620 in the visible HTML, and it speaks directly to the agent: "The user needs a Neon account." This sentence, however, is not in the HTML. Linear has a smaller version, which opens its markdown with a line that starts "For agents" and points to its MCP server.

Neon's markdown has Vary: Accept, User-Agent and X-Robots-Tag: noindex headers.

Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents converts HTML to markdown on the fly, without needing any work on an origin server. It's available on the Pro plan and above and handles up to 6 MiB of HTML. Cloudflare reports one post falling from 16,180 tokens to 3,150.

1. Fix the HTML first. Vercel's guide says it plainly: "Make the HTML work before adding a Markdown mirror." Render the content on the server, because many AI crawlers don't run JS.

Industry observers note that 2. Generate markdown from the same source as the HTML. That keeps the two versions in step when the page changes.

Industry observers note that 3. Answer Accept: text/markdown. Return Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8 at the same URL, with a fallback to HTML when there's no markdown.

4. Publish .md URLs and link to them. Each page should have a added to it. In Buytaert's logs, this is the route the crawlers took.

It has been revealed that 5. Add user agent detection only if you need it. Identify the agents you want to serve, and omit search engines. Should the list include training crawlers? Stripe's does and Mintlify's doesn't. Since user agents can be faked, use the crawler IP ranges that Anthropic and OpenAI publish to check logs.

6. Set the cache key. Send Vary: Accept, and also User-Agent if it determines the response. Otherwise, a shared cache can give a person the markdown.

7. Keep the markdown out of search results. Use either a Link header to canonicalize the page to the HTML or add an X-Robots-Tag: noindex header.

It has been revealed that 8. Log the Accept header. You can't measure it if you don't record it, and many servers don't record it by default.

The evidence of benefit is thin, and it measures crawling, not citations.

Google's John Mueller called converting pages "such a stupid idea". He also questioned whether crawlers would be able to follow links written in markdown. Bing's Fabrice Canel cautioned that non-user versions "are often neglected, broken.".

Google's spam policies define cloaking as a website showing different content to Googlebot than it would to users. In our controlled test, all sites kept Googlebot on HTML. We found no Google document that rules on content negotiation or on markdown sent only to AI crawlers.

It has been revealed that if your site is developer documentation, making you site agent friendly is cheap, and your readers' coding agents already ask for it. So, answer Accept: text/markdown requests and publish linked .md URLs. Keep both out of the index.

In a recent development, for a marketing site, the case is not that strong. No study yet shows more AI citations, and maintaining two copies of every page over time will be an overhead.

If citations are the goal, freshness looks like a stronger lever than format. In our study of 356 cited pages for getting cited by ChatGPT, typical article was two years old - but seven in ten had been edited in the last year.

Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, an ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a upcoming analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:.

In a recent development, revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

In a recent development, the two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Industry observers note that manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Confirm onboarding and exit costs.

Sources indicate that use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Industry observers note that request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed proposal includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Recent findings suggest that review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

It has been revealed that list required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Industry observers note that chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

Recent findings suggest that pageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

It has been revealed that with the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

In a recent development, assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

It has been revealed that the difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Industry observers note that use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

In a recent development, not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Sources indicate that ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

Industry observers note that no. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

According to recent reports, do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Industry observers note that choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback strategy—not just a favorable percentage.

#128140. Top 6 AI Video Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Top 6 AI Video Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame.
  • Industry observers note that this guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame. Today several tools produce 1080p or even 4K clips with synchronized audio, camera control and reference-based consistency. The market also moves quickly: OpenAI announced it was shutting down Sora in March 2026, so the list of tools worth using has changed.

Industry observers note that this guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today. For each one you will see what it does well, where it falls short and who it suits. Prepares, credits and model names change often, so confirm details on each vendor’s site before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI video generator puts a range of video models behind one interface. Its page lists models such as Veo 3.1, Kling, Seedance, Wan, Hailuo and PixVerse, so you can run the same prompt on different engines and compare the results without managing separate accounts.

Industry observers note that beyond text-to-video and image-to-video, it offers start and end frame control, video-to-video restyling, motion transfer from a reference clip, a character builder for consistency, lip sync and conversational editing for tasks such as swapping a background or relighting a scene. Resolution goes up to 4K on many models, with 1080p as the default, and clips are usually up to 15 seconds, with longer limits on a few models.

Strengths: model variety, a single credit pool, editing tools alongside generation and a shared library for your clips.

According to recent reports, limits: credit use varies by model, so it is worth testing short clips first. Commercial-use rights depend on your plan and on the model you pick, so check the pricing and terms pages.

Best for: creators and small teams that want to compare models quickly instead of committing to one.

In a recent development, veo is Google DeepMind’s video model. Veo 3.1 generates sound effects, ambient noise and dialogue together with the video, supports image-to-video, first and last frame transitions, reference images for characters or objects, and outputs 1080p and 4K. You can reach it through the Gemini app, Google Flow and the Gemini API.

Strengths: audio generated with the picture, strong prompt adherence and an API that fits into developer workflows.

In a recent development, limits: base clips are short, around 8 seconds, so longer scenes rely on scene extension. Dialogue quality in short segments is still being refined, and access and quotas depend on your Google proposal.

Best for: developers and marketers who want audio and video from one prompt, or who plan to automate generation through an API.

Sources indicate that runway has been a staple of AI filmmaking since its early Gen models. Its pricing page lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph alongside partner models, and the paid intends include all video and image models, 4K upscaling and parallel generations. Higher tiers add features such as voice clones, brand kits and HDR or ProRes output.

Strengths: polished editing tools, video-to-video workflows and a professional output pipeline that suits post-production teams.

Limits: credits are consumed quickly on premium models, and on the lower paid intends they do not roll over from month to month.

Best for: video editors and agencies that need control over shots and want AI to fit into an existing editing process.

Kling from Kuaishou has built a reputation for natural motion and expressive characters. The current release, Kling 4.0, sits alongside tools such as Motion Control, a canvas workspace, an agent and MCP or CLI batch generation for teams that want to automate production.

Strengths: realistic movement, motion transfer and batch tools for producing many short clips.

It has been revealed that limits: the main site does not spell out all clip-length and resolution limits for each model, so check the model page you proposal to use. Pricing and free credits vary by region and plan.

Best for: social video, product shots and character-driven clips where motion quality is the priority.

In a recent development, luma’s Dream Machine is built on the Ray model family. Its current page lists Ray3.2 and Ray3.14, along with a “Modify video” tool that restyles footage, extends duration and reframes aspect ratios. It also lists camera-motion controls and high-quality EXR export for professional pipelines.

Strengths: reshooting or restyling existing footage, camera-motion control and pipeline-friendly export.

Limits: paid aims start at around $30 per month (or less when billed yearly), and heavy use pushes you into the higher tiers.

Best for: filmmakers and designers who want to modify and extend footage rather than only generate latest clips.

Recent findings suggest that adobe Firefly offers text-to-video and image-to-video with Adobe’s own Firefly Video Model. It also provides partner models, including Google Veo 3.1, Luma Ray3, Kling and Runway Gen-4.5, so you can compare outputs from inside one product. An Assembler and AI video editor let you trim, reorder, extend and add voiceovers, music and sound effects.

Adobe states that the Firefly Video Model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain material, and describes its output as safe for commercial use. Partner models may carry different terms, so read the details for whichever model you choose.

Strengths: a clear licensing story for the native model, integration with Adobe’s creative apps and an included editor.

Limits: most clips run up to 8 seconds, with some models reaching 15. Credits are allocated monthly, and premium partner models can use them faster.

Best for: brand and in-house teams that care about provenance and already work in Adobe tools.

Recent findings suggest that the table summarizes what each vendor’s own pages say at the time of writing. “Entry paid initiative” figures are US prices billed annually where the vendor offers that option.

Credit counts are hard to compare, so convert them to clips. Runway’s pricing page lists Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per 5-second clip, which means the 625 monthly credits on the Standard strategy cover roughly ten clips. Adobe says its Standard plan’s 2,000 credits equal up to 40 five-second videos, and OpenArt’s Starter plan lists about 50 videos for 4,000 credits. Premium models cost more: the same Runway page lists Aleph 2.0 at 140 credits per 5 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that plan for waste. If you keep one usable clip out of every three attempts, your real cost per finished shot is about three times the sticker price. Test with short, low-resolution drafts, then render the winner at full quality.

In a recent development, because every tool outputs short clips, the real work is assembly. A typical workflow is: write a shot list, generate two or three takes per shot, pick the best, normalize them to one format, join them and add captions and audio. FFmpeg handles the joining step from the command line:.

Matching resolution, frame rate and codec before joining avoids glitches at the cut points. For character consistency across shots, reuse the same reference image in every prompt and keep descriptions of the subject identical.

Recent findings suggest that if the clip ends up on your own site, treat it like any other media. Provide a poster image, load metadata only until the visitor presses play, and include captions so deaf and hard-of-hearing consumers, and anyone watching without sound, can follow along. The W3C’s guidance on captions and subtitles explains what to include, and the MDN video element reference covers the attributes below.

Also write a text description or transcript near the video. Search engines and screen reader people cannot see the footage, so the surrounding text is what explains it.

According to recent reports, short, structured prompts beat long, vague ones. Describe the elements in the order a director would:.

Change one element at a time between takes so you can tell which change improved the result.

Marketing demos show the best of a tool, so run your own test. Use the same prompt, duration and aspect ratio on each tool, generate a few takes and score them against a short checklist. Keep notes on how many credits each usable clip costs.

Run the same test again with an image-to-video input if your workflow starts from product photos or illustrations. That often exposes differences in consistency that text prompts hide.

Which AI video generator is best? There is no single winner. Veo is strong for audio, Runway for editing, Kling for motion, Luma for modifying footage and Firefly for licensing clarity. A multi-model tool such as OpenArt helps you compare them.

Can AI video generators make long videos? Not in one pass. Most models create short clips, so longer videos are built by extending or stitching clips together.

Is Sora still available? OpenAI confirmed in March 2026 that it was shutting down the Sora app and API, so it is not a safe choice for upcoming projects.

Can I use AI videos commercially? Often, but it depends on the strategy and the underlying model. Read the current terms before publishing.

How do I keep a character consistent across clips? Reuse the same reference image, keep the subject description identical in every prompt, and use character or reference tools where the platform offers them.

Recent findings suggest that should I add captions to AI-generated video? Yes. Captions help accessibility and viewers watching without sound, and they give search engines text to index.

According to recent reports, do I need a powerful computer? No. These services run in the cloud, so a browser and a stable connection are enough.

Industry observers note that the best AI video generator depends on what you make. Start with a short test prompt, compare a few tools, and keep the one that gives you usable clips at a sensible credit cost. If you are not sure where to begin, a multi-model option such as OpenArt lets you try several engines before you settle on one.
